title: Mandela & Margaret Thatcher: When These Views Were Considered Civilized
summary: When Thatcher lectured him against nationalization, Mandela smiled: 'When I entered prison in 1964, these policies were considered civilized across the world; in fact, we learned them from your British Parliament!'
keywords: Mandela & Margaret Thatcher: When These Views Were Considered Civilized
full_text:
In July 1990, Nelson Mandela arrived at 10 Downing Street in London to meet British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.

Thatcher, the 'Iron Lady' of free-market capitalism, strongly disapproved of the African National Congress's commitment to nationalizing South African mines and financial institutions.

Prior to the meeting, British diplomat Lord Renwick warned Mandela: "Be prepared, Mr. Mandela; the Prime Minister intends to give you a stern lecture on modern economics!"

During the meeting, Thatcher spoke forcefully:
"Mr. Mandela, you have emerged into a transformed world. Socialism and nationalization have failed completely. Free markets govern the globe. You must abandon these outdated nationalization policies immediately!"

Mandela listened with profound calm and an amused smile.

When Thatcher paused, Mandela responded in his low, measured timbre:
"Prime Minister, I have listened to you with great care.
However, you must remember: I entered Robben Island prison in 1964.
In those days, public ownership of key utilities and the nationalization of basic resources were considered the height of civilized democratic policy! In truth, my colleagues and I learned those very social democratic ideas from your own British Labour Party and British parliamentary history!
Having just emerged from prison, we must examine your modern economic doctrines with careful deliberation!"

Thatcher paused, taken aback by Mandela's historical retort, and broke into an appreciative smile.

No matter how intimidating the world leaders he faced, Mandela's mastery of historical context and gentle irony commanded unconditional respect.
moral: Meeting conservative lectures with historical irony and unwavering dignity, Mandela proved that revolutionary patience disarms imperial lecturing.
